In mathematics, the '''complex hyperbolic space''' is a [[Hermitian manifold]] which is the equivalent of the [[real hyperbolic space]] in the context of [[complex manifolds]]. The complex hyperbolic space is a [[Kähler manifold]], and it is characterised by being the only [[simply connected]] [[complete manifold|complete]] Kähler manifold whose [[holomorphic sectional curvature]] is constant equal to &minus;1. Its underlying [[Riemannian manifold]] has non-constant negative curvature, pinched between &minus;1 and &minus;1/4, or between &minus;4 and &minus;1, according to the choice of a normalization of the metric): in particular, it is a [[CAT(k) space|CAT(&minus;1/4) space]].

The complex hyperbolic space is also the [[symmetric space]] associated with the [[Lie group]] <math>\operatorname{PU}(n,1)</math>. These spaces constitute one of the three families of rank one symmetric spaces, together with real and quaternionic hyperbolic spaces, classification to which must be added one exceptional space, the [[Cayley plane]]. It is also the only family of Hermitian symmetric spaces having rank one.

== Construction of the complex hyperbolic space ==

=== Projective model ===
Let <math>\langle u,v\rangle := -u_1\overline{v_1} + u_2\overline{v_2} + \dots + u_{n+1}\overline{v_{n+1}}</math> be a [[Sesquilinear form|pseudo-Hermitian form]] of signature <math>(n,1)</math> in the complex [[vector space]] <math>\mathbb{C}^{n+1}</math>. The projective model of the complex hyperbolic space is the [[Complex projective space|projectivized space]] of all negative vectors for this form: <math>\mathbb{H}^n_\mathbb{C} =  \{[\xi] \in \mathbb{CP}^n \mid \langle \xi,\xi\rangle <0\}.</math>

As an open set of the complex projective space, this space is endowed with the structure of a [[complex manifold]]. It is [[Biholomorphism|biholomorphic]] to the unit ball of <math>\mathbb{C}^n</math>, because every negative complex line is spanned by a unique vector of the form <math>(1,x_1,\dots,x_n)</math> with <math>\sum_{i=1}^{n} |x_i|^2 < 1</math>. The map sending the point <math>(x_1,\dots,x_n)</math> of the unit ball of <math>\mathbb{C}^n</math> to the point <math>[1:x_1:\dots:x_n]</math> of the projective space thus defines a biholomorphism.

This model is the equivalent of the [[Poincaré disk model]]. Unlike the real hyperbolic space, the complex projective space cannot be defined as a connected component of the hyperboloid <math>\langle x,x\rangle = -1</math>, because the projection of this hyperboloid onto the projective model has connected fiber <math>\mathbb{S}^1</math> (the fiber being <math>\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}</math> in the real case).

A [[Hermitian metric]] is defined on <math>\mathbb{H}^n_\mathbb{C}</math> in the following way: if <math>p\in \C^{n+1}</math> belongs to the cone <math>\langle p,p\rangle=-1</math>, then the restriction of <math>\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle </math> to the orthogonal space <math>(\C p)^{\perp} \subset \C^{n+1}</math> defines a definite positive hermitian product on this space, and because the [[tangent space]] of <math>\mathbb{H}^n_\mathbb{C}</math> at the point <math>[p]</math> can be naturally identified with <math>(\C p)^{\perp}</math>, this defines a hermitian inner product on <math>T_{[p]}\mathbb{H}^n_\mathbb{C}</math>. As can be seen by computation, this inner product does not depend on the choice of the representative <math>p</math>. In order to have holomorphic sectional curvature equal to -1 and not -4, one needs to renormalize this metric by a  factor of <math>1/2</math>. This metric is a [[Kähler metric]].

===Siegel model===
The Siegel model of complex hyperbolic space is the subset of <math>(w,z)\in\mathbb C\times\mathbb C^{n-1}</math> such that
:<math>i(\bar w-w) > 2z\bar z.</math>
It is biholomorphic to the unit ball in <math>\mathbb C^n</math> via the [[Cayley transform]]
:<math>(w,z)\mapsto \left(\frac{w-i}{w+i},\frac{2z}{w+i}\right).</math>

===Boundary at infinity===

In the projective model, the complex hyperbolic space identifies with the complex unit ball of dimension <math>n</math>, and its boundary can be defined as the boundary of the ball, which is diffeomorphic to the sphere of real dimension <math>2n-1</math>. This is equivalent to defining:
<math>\partial\mathbb{H}^n_\mathbb{C} =  \{[\xi] \in \mathbb{CP}^n | \langle \xi,\xi\rangle =0\}.</math>

As a [[CAT(k) space|CAT(0) space]], the complex hyperbolic space also has a boundary at infinity <math>\partial_{\infty}\mathbb{H}^n_\mathbb{C}</math>. This boundary coincides with the boundary <math>\partial\mathbb{H}^n_\mathbb{C}</math> just defined.

The boundary of the complex hyperbolic space naturally carries a [[CR-structure|CR structure]]. This structure is also the standard [[contact structure]] on the (odd dimensional) sphere.

==Group of holomorphic isometries and symmetric space==

The group of holomorphic isometries of the complex hyperbolic space is the [[Lie group]] <math>\operatorname{PU}(n,1)</math>. This group acts transitively on the complex hyperbolic space, and the stabilizer of a point is isomorphic to the unitary group <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math>. The complex hyperbolic space is thus [[homeomorphic]] to the [[homogeneous space]] <math>\operatorname{PU}(n,1)/\operatorname{U}(n)</math>. The stabilizer <math>\operatorname{U}(n)</math> is the [[maximal compact subgroup]] of <math>\operatorname{PU}(n,1)</math>.

As a consequence, the complex hyperbolic space is the [[Riemannian symmetric space]] <math>\operatorname{SU}(n,1)/\mathrm{S}(\operatorname{U}(n)\times \operatorname{U}(1))=\operatorname{PU}(n,1)/\operatorname{U}(n)</math>,<ref>{{citation|last = Besse | first = Arthur | author-link=Arthur Besse|title=Einstein manifolds|page=180|year=1987|publisher=Springer}}.</ref> where <math>\operatorname{SU}(n,1)</math> is the pseudo-unitary group and <math>\operatorname{PU}(n,1)</math> is the quotient of <math>\operatorname{SU}(n,1)</math> by its [[Center (group theory)|center]], which is isomorphic to <math>\Z/(n+1)\Z</math>.

The group of holomorphic isometries of the complex hyperbolic space also acts on the boundary of this space, and acts thus by homeomorphisms on the closed disk <math>\bar{\mathbb{D}} = \mathbb{H}^n_{\mathbb{C}} \cup \partial\mathbb{H}^n_{\mathbb{C}}</math>. By [[Brouwer's fixed point theorem]], any holomorphic isometry of the complex hyperbolic space must fix at least one point in <math>\bar{\mathbb{D}}</math>. There is a classification of isometries into three types:<ref name="CNS">{{harvtxt|Cano|Navarrete|Seade|2013}}</ref>
* An isometry is said to be elliptic if it fixes a point in the complex hyperbolic space.
* An isometry is said to be parabolic if it does not fix a point in the complex hyperbolic space and fixes a unique point in the boundary.
* An isometry is said to be hyperbolic (or loxodromic) if it does not fix a point in the complex hyperbolic space and fixes exactly two points in the boundary.

The [[Iwasawa decomposition]] of <math>\operatorname{PU}(n,1)</math> is the decomposition <math>\operatorname{PU}(n,1)=K\times A\times N</math>, where <math>K=\operatorname{U}(n)</math> is the [[unitary group]], <math>A=\mathbb{R}</math> is the additive group of real numbers and <math>N=\mathcal{H_n}</math> is the [[Heisenberg group]] of real dimension <math>2n-1</math>. Such a decomposition depends on the choice of:
* A point <math>\xi</math> in the boundary of the complex hyperbolic space (<math>N</math> is then the group of [[unipotent]] parabolic elements of <math>\operatorname{PU}(n,1)</math> fixing <math>\xi</math>)
* An oriented [[geodesic]] line <math>\ell</math> going to <math>\xi </math> at infinity (<math>A</math> is then the group of hyperbolic elements of <math>\operatorname{PU}(n,1)</math> acting as a translation along this geodesic and with no rotational part around it)
* The choice of an origin for <math>\ell</math>, i.e. a unit speed parametrization <math>\gamma:\R\to \mathbb{H}^n_{\mathbb{C}} </math> whose image is <math>\ell</math> (<math>K</math> is then the group of elliptic elements of <math>\operatorname{PU}(n,1)</math> fixing <math>\gamma(0)</math>)

For any such decomposition of <math>\operatorname{PU}(n,1)</math>, the action of the subgroup <math>A\times N</math> is free and transitive, hence induces a diffeomorphism <math>A\times N \to \mathbb{H}^n_{\mathbb{C}}</math>. This diffeomorphism can be seen as a generalization of the Siegel model.

==Curvature==

The group of holomorphic isometries <math>\operatorname{PU}(n,1)</math> acts [[Group action|transitively]] on the tangent complex lines of the hyperbolic complex space. This is why this space has constant [[holomorphic sectional curvature]], that can be computed to be equal to -4 (with the above normalization of the metric). This property characterizes the hyperbolic complex space: up to isometric biholomorphism, there is only one [[Simply connected space|simply connected]] complete [[Kähler manifold]] of given constant [[holomorphic sectional curvature]].<ref name="Besse">{{harvtxt|Besse|1987}}</ref>

Furthermore, when a Hermitian manifold has constant holomorphic sectional curvature equal to <math>k</math>, the sectional curvature of every real tangent plane <math>\Pi</math> is completely determined by the formula:

<math>K(\Pi) = \frac{k}{4}\left(1+3\cos^2(\alpha(\Pi)\right)</math>

where <math>\alpha(\Pi)</math> is the angle between <math>\Pi</math> and <math>J\Pi</math>, ie the infimum of the angles between a vector in <math>\Pi</math> and a vector in <math>J\Pi</math>.<ref name="Besse" /> This angle equals 0 [[if and only if]] <math>\Pi</math> is a complex line, and equals <math>\pi/2</math> if and only if <math>\Pi</math> is totally real. Thus the sectional curvature of the complex hyperbolic space varies from -4 (for complex lines) to -1 (for totally real planes).

In complex dimension 1, every real plane in the tangent space is a complex line: thus the hyperbolic complex space of dimension 1 has constant curvature equal to -1, and by the [[uniformization theorem]], it is isometric to the real hyperbolic plane. Hyperbolic complex spaces can thus be seen as another high-dimensional generalization of the hyperbolic plane, less standard than the real hyperbolic spaces. A third possible generalization is the [[homogeneous space]] <math>SL_n(\mathbb{R})/SO_n(\mathbb{\R})</math>, which for <math>n=2</math> again coincides with the hyperbolic plane, but becomes a symmetric space of rank greater than 1 when <math>n\ge 3</math>.

==Totally geodesic subspaces==

Every totally geodesic submanifold of the complex hyperbolic space of dimension n is one of the following:
* a copy of a complex hyperbolic space of smaller dimension
* a copy of a real hyperbolic space of real dimension smaller than <math>n</math>
In particular, there is no codimension 1 totally geodesic subspace of the complex hyperbolic space.

==Link with other metrics on the ball==

* On the unit ball, the complex hyperbolic metric coincides, up to some scalar renormalization, with the [[Bergman metric]]. This implies that every biholomorphism of the ball is actually an isometry of the complex hyperbolic metric.
* The complex hyperbolic metric also coincides with the [[Kobayashi metric]].
* Up to renormalization, the complex hyperbolic metric is [[Kähler–Einstein metric|Kähler-Einstein]], which means that its [[Ricci curvature]] is a multiple of the metric.
